newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Vote counting under way after Pakistan polls.
newsitem.headline: Vote counting under way after Pakistan polls.

text.p: Vote counting began in Pakistan on Monday after an apparently dismal turnout for an election expected to return former prime minister Nawaz Sharif to power.
Seven people were killed in election day violence, but officials said polling was generally peaceful in a lacklustre contest between Sharif and his ousted rival Benazir Bhutto.
Many of Pakistan's 56.5 million eligible voters seemed to have stayed away, either because of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan or because they distrust current political leaders.
First results were expected by 10 p.m. (1700 GMT), with the outcome clear by 2 a.m.or 3 a.m. on Tuesday(2100 to 2200 GMT on Monday).
Five people were shot dead when two groups at odds over a land dispute clashed near a polling station in Gujranwala, in the central province of Punjab, police said.
In the southern city of Karachi, two supporters of the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) were killed and three were wounded, MQM sources and ambulance workers said.
President Farooq Leghari called national and provincial assembly elections, being held on the same day for the first time, after dismissing Bhutto on November 5.
He accused her government of corruption, nepotism and extra-judicial killings in Karachi and the Supreme Court ruled last week that the president's action had been justified.

About 250,000 troops were deployed for the elections, which were monitored by observers from the United States, European Union, Commonwealth and South Asia, as well as the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan. Several polling stations opened late.
Nawaz Sharif, widely tipped to be next prime minister, said he was confident of winning a clear parliamentary majority.
But if the turnout proves as low as many believe, it may be hard for any new government to claim a credible popular mandate, threatening Pakistan with further political instability.

"The country needs a strong and stable government," said Sharif, who served as prime minister from 1990 to 1993, when he was sacked by the president, restored by the Supreme Court and then persuaded to resign before losing a general election.
He promised not to seek revenge on Bhutto for alleged victimisation of his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) while she was in power and said he would not put her on trial.
"We are not going to indulge in any politics of revenge," he told Reuters. "It will be clean, good politics and we'll try to seek her cooperation to take the country forward."
He said the opposition and government should have a working relationship. "So what she did to us, we will not do to her."
Bhutto, who went to vote at 8 a.m. in a primary school in her village of Naudero, in Sindh province, was visibly surprised to find that she was the first to cast a ballot there.
"People are voting for the arrow because they want stability, they want democracy," she said, referring to the election symbol of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
Ghinwa Bhutto, Lebanese-born widow of Benazir's slain brother Murtaza and now leader of the PPP faction he founded, was also the first person to vote in her Larkana constituency.
Pakistan's cricketer-turned- politician Imran Khan failed to cast what would have been his first vote in an election.
"Unfortunately the Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) could not field a candidate in my constituency so therefore I am abstaining," he told reporters in Mianwali, his home town.
"It was a question of either voting for the Muslim League or the People's Party. Neither of the two parties I feel have done justice in the past and I do not expect wonders from them now."
Imran is standing in nine other constituencies for his Tehrik-i-Insaaf, as permitted under Pakistan's electoral law.
Leghari pledged a swift transfer of power to a new government and denied charges by Bhutto, a former ally and now a bitter foe, that he planned to rig voting in 65 constituencies.
"There will no delay in the transfer of power even by a single day," Leghari said. "There should be no confusion."
State radio quoted him as saying that the National Assembly would be called to elect a new prime minister after the Election Commission notifies official election results in mid-February.
